main.job: makes a question sound engaged and natural rather than blunt
main.why: Most frequent particle in spoken questions; learners hear it constantly and questions without it can sound cold.

main.job: softens an imperative or request into a casual 'just/quickly'
main.why: Everyday requests (Kannst du mal…, Guck mal) use it constantly; the easiest particle to start producing.

main.job: turns an imperative into a friendly nudge or invitation: 'why don't you…'
main.why: Komm doch mit! / Setz dich doch! are core polite-invitation forms.

main.job: marks a statement as something both speakers already know or can see
main.why: Extremely frequent in statements; unstressed ja is not 'yes' and learners misread it.

main.job: in a statement: 'but you know that / I told you', reminding or mild reproach
main.why: Das weißt du doch! is everyday; separate job from the suggestion doch (R-TERM-05).

main.job: shifts a question to a new topic or asks what someone 'actually' does: 'by the way'
main.why: Was machst du eigentlich beruflich? — standard small-talk topic shift.
Das klappt schon / Das wird schon — high frequency comfort phrase pattern.

main.job: presents something as a plain fact you can't change; shrugging acceptance
main.why: Very common in colloquial speech across Germany, Austria and the south; learners hear it all the time.

spares.job: same shrug as halt, more northern and slightly more standard
spares.why: Next in frequency; regional twin of halt.
Nimm dir ruhig noch was — common hospitality particle.

spares.job: in exclamations: surprise at what you see
spares.why: Das ist ja toll! — second frequent job of ja.

shape.notes: Grammar slice: every item is a particle tied to one job, spread across the three sentence types particles live in (questions, requests, statements). Modal particles are not a small closed set (~15 core members), so no set is declared. No nouns.
